reports.summary:
I measured cost and speed at 5,000 documents on a seen set: mt5k's 5,089 documents, copied to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/u5k/scale/probe. Both banks build, and nothing crashed or timed out on 100 planner answers (v13 and v4, 50 questions each) or on 50 untrained v1 asks.

- **Cost per question:** about 5 s with v13 and 6.4 s with v4, against about 0.18 to 0.2 s at 50 documents.
- **Where the time goes:** mostly `FactBank.named`, the alias lookup. One call takes 0.46 s at 5k against 1 ms at 50 documents. The bank has 7,929 aliases, more than Python's 512-entry regex cache holds, so every call recompiles every pattern.
- **A crash in the pipeline:** `factbank_split changed` fails at 5k with IndexError. It has to rename 4,008 people but has only 560 fresh names.
- **Full run estimate:** about 2.6 CPU-hours for the arms; with setup, about 3 h on one core or about 1 h with 4 arms in parallel. This is a rough estimate, and it assumes the changed copy is fixed first.
- **Score hint (seen set, not a test):** v13 0.859 against 1.000 at 50 documents, v4 0.577 against 0.647. 12 of v13's 15 wrong answers come from one mismatch: the wording says "tickets", but the expected answers count Linear issues only, and at 5k people also hold Jira tickets.
- **Kept:** the two .sqlite files total 221 MB, under the 300 MB limit, so they stay in the probe folder.

findings.title: Build: both banks build; the first build's wall time was mostly cold file reads
findings.detail:
`factbank_test build` on 5,089 documents. The checker passed for both banks, with no errors and no contradictions.
- **v1:** 152.6 s wall but only 11.4 s CPU, so it was waiting on cold file reads. My question generation and another lens were reading documents at the same time.
- **v2 (`--text-facts`):** 16.1 s wall with a warm cache.
- **Peak RAM:** 475 MB and 510 MB. The machine has 14 GB free.
- **At 50 documents** the same builds took 0.65 s and 1.64 s.
- Timing files: build_v1_time.json and build_v2_time.json in u5k/scale.
findings.numbers: v1: 152.6 s wall (8.2 user + 3.2 sys), 475 MB RAM, 109,528 facts, 15,300 entities, 106.0 MB. v2: 16.1 s wall (13.5 user + 2.3 sys), 510 MB RAM, 130,184 facts, 115.0 MB. Together 221 MB. At 50 docs: 1.83 MB and 2.04 MB.

findings.title: Questions at 5k: loading is slow, generating is instant
findings.detail:
`questions(docs, set(dsids), True, 1, wordings=load_wordings(.../factbank_order/wordings.json))` gave 50 questions:
- action items 9, compare 8, issue_pr_author 1, person_count 8, person_first 8, pr_issue 8, ticket_link 8.
- Without the cap there are 193.
- Units found: person 42, ticket 64, pr 14, action 29.
- Loading the 5,089 documents took 103 s wall but 3.8 s CPU (cold disk). Generating took under 0.1 s. Peak RAM 199 MB.
- 2 of 139 PR numbers are shared by two documents.
- Written to probe/questions.jsonl; details in questions_info.json.
findings.numbers: load 103.4 s; units+questions <0.1 s; 50 questions (193 uncapped); 199 MB RAM

findings.title: Per-question time: about 25 to 30 times slower than at 50 documents, no crashes or timeouts
findings.detail:
Each question was answered as `ask_plans` does it: `plans.answer`, then the evidence head and `tb.ask`, with one planner per arm.
- **v13:** mean 4.97 s, median 4.34, p90 6.96, max 9.77. The answer step averaged 3.09 s and the evidence step 1.88 s. By group: link 4.8 s, combine 4.3 s, compare 7.5 s.
- **v4:** mean 6.36 s, median 5.66, p90 9.83, max 17.66.
- **v1 (`FactBank.ask`):** mean 0.78 s, max 1.15 s.
- **At 50 documents (mdord):** v13 177 ms, v4 195 ms, v1 8 ms.
- **Cross-check with the real CLI:** `factbank_multi ask` with v13 on the probe took 248.1 s wall (243 s CPU) for 50 questions. Peak RAM 210.5 MB, output 1.27 MB, and the answers matched the in-memory run on 50 of 50.
- No exceptions or timeouts in 150 asks. RAM per arm process was about 210 MB, so 4 parallel arms fit easily.

findings.title: The hot path is FactBank.named, then scoring the candidates
findings.detail:
`named()` runs one regex per alias, and the bank has 7,929 aliases. That is more than Python's 512-entry regex cache holds, so every call recompiles every pattern.
- One call takes 0.46 s at 5k against 1 ms at 50 documents (184 aliases).
- **v13:** about 5.2 calls per answer step, taking 2.58 s of the 3.09 s answer time.
- **v4:** about 7.6 calls, taking 3.88 s of 4.48 s.
- The evidence step (`tb.ask`) calls `named()` at least twice more. I got that from reading the code, not from timing it.
- **The slowest questions** are the ones whose answer appears in the question (compare questions, and keys named by two documents). Scoring each candidate (`Planner.x` → `offers_choice`) then calls `named()` again. Examples: v4 ticket_link-status-092 took 17.7 s with 27 calls (14.0 s in `named`); v13 compare_two-192 took 9.6 s with 14 calls (6.9 s).
- **Without `named()`**, enumerating candidates (`candidates`/`execute`) costs about 0.5 to 0.6 s per question.
- **Candidate plans:** v13 mean 586 (median 567, range 178 to 1,282), and 26.6 left after the checks (median 11, max 266). v4 mean 605, max 1,321, all of them scored.
findings.numbers: named(): 0.46 s/call at 5k vs 0.001 s at 50 docs; 52% of v13 total time from the answer step alone; candidates mean 586 (v13), 605 (v4)

findings.title: Crash: the changed copy cannot be built at 5k
findings.detail:
`python -m cie.eval.factbank_split changed --work <probe>` fails at factbank_split.py line 193 with IndexError: list index out of range.
- The 5,089 documents have 4,008 people to rename, but FIRST × LAST gives only 560 fresh names.
- Nothing was written before it failed.
- **Renaming is also slow:** `rename()` loops over every name for every string. On 100 sampled documents, with 4,008 stand-in names, it took 10.1 s. That extrapolates to about 515 s for 5,089 documents (136,237 strings).
- The changed copy would also write about 31 MB of documents and a second pair of banks (about 221 MB).
findings.numbers: 4,008 people vs 560 names; about 515 s estimated rename time; changed_probe.json

findings.title: Scores, as a rough hint only (seen set)
findings.detail:
**v13:** 0.859 (link 0.824, combine 0.753, compare 1.000), right for the right reason 0.740. On the first 20 questions alone, 0.882.
**v4:** 0.577 (link 0.412, combine 0.320, compare 1.000), right for the right reason 0.371.
**At 50 documents (mdord):** v13 1.000, v4 0.647.

Why v13 got 15 questions wrong:
- **12: the wording says "tickets", the expected answers count Linear only.** Since v11, "ticket" means Linear or Jira, and at 5k these people hold Jira tickets too. I checked the 4 person_count questions: v13's counts (Jordan Lee 4, Marcus Li 5, Ravi Kapoor 3, Priya Nair 6) are exactly each person's Linear plus Jira tickets. The 8 action-item answers add INT-/SUP- Jira keys. I checked Priya Nair's set; I did not check the others one by one.
- **2: the benchmark reuses ticket keys.** 38 of the 7,929 aliases name more than one entity. SUP-24871 is the key of two Jira documents, and ENG-4829 of four Linear documents. The generator and the bank's `resolve()` each pick one of them arbitrarily, and they may pick different ones. In ticket_link-status-092 the key named two documents, so the choice check misfired. In ticket_link-assignee-086, ENG-314159 resolved to another document.
- **1: the word "email" in the wording.** "for the status email" names gmail as a system, and at 5k there are Gmail documents referencing the issue, so the plan ended there (pr_issue-due_date-085).

findings.title: Estimate for a full run: 7 arms × 50 questions × (test set + changed copy + 3 single-writer sets)
findings.detail:
**Arms, CPU time per set:**
- v4 and v8 at about 318 s each (v8 assumed to cost like v4, not measured).
- v9, v11, v12, v13 and v14 at about 248 s each.
- That is 1,876 s, about 31 min per set, so 5 sets need about 2.6 CPU-hours.

**Setup on top of that:**
- Builds: about 150 s cold plus 16 s warm, for the test set and for the changed copy.
- v1 asks: 2 × 39 s.
- Changed copy: about 515 s of renaming, once its crash is fixed.
- Loading documents for the draw and the single-writer script: about 100 to 400 s cold.
- The 50-document guard sets: about 4 min, as in run_order.log.

**Total:** about 3 to 3.2 h on one core. With 4 arm processes in parallel on an otherwise idle machine, about 1 h wall.

**Not included:** the 3B model's form calls for v12 and v14 (250 new questions), which I did not time.

**Disk:** banks for the test set and the changed copy about 442 MB, changed documents about 31 MB, answer files about 1.27 MB per arm per set (about 45 MB). About 520 MB in all; 1.6 GB is free now.
findings.numbers: about 9,400 s of arms + about 1,500 to 2,000 s of setup = about 3 h on one core; about 1 h with 4 in parallel; about 520 MB disk

findings.title: Where the files are
findings.detail:
Kept in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/u5k/scale/:
- **probe/:** factbank.sqlite (106.0 MB) and factbank_v2.sqlite (115.0 MB), 221 MB together, which is under the 300 MB limit. Also haystack.json (mt5k's 5,089 dsids), the index.json symlink, questions.jsonl, and factbank_v13.jsonl (the CLI arm's output).
- **Results:** ans_v13.jsonl, ans_v4.jsonl, ans_v1.jsonl (per question: times, inner timings, call counts, candidate counts, answers, scores), questions_info.json, changed_probe.json, build_v1_time.json, build_v2_time.json, cli_v13_time.json.
- **Scripts:** timed.py, gen_questions.py, answer_probe.py, changed_probe.py, analyse.py.

The folder is 213 MB in all. No repository file was changed.
findings.numbers: 213 MB in u5k/scale

recommendations: Before the pre-registration, fix `factbank_split.changed` for 5k documents. It needs enough fresh names for about 4,000 people (or should rename only the people the questions use). Its `rename()` should also stop looping over every name for every string, for example by using one compiled regex. Freeze the fix and check that it reproduces the existing 50-document changed copies byte for byte.

Fix the 5k question set before drawing it. Either compute person_count and action-item answers over Linear and Jira together (which is what the "tickets" wordings and v11/v13 mean), or use wordings that say "Linear". Also drop any unit whose ticket key or PR number is carried by more than one document. At 5k, 38 aliases name more than one entity, and 2 of 139 PR numbers are shared.

Consider a pre-freeze fix of `FactBank.named`: one precompiled alternation, or a token lookup. It takes about 0.46 s per call at 5k and makes up about 50 to 75% of each question's time. The fix must give the same `named()` output on every earlier set (diff the answers files). Without it, the full run still fits in about 3 h on one core.
Run the arm processes 4 at a time. Each needs about 210 MB of RAM and is CPU-bound, so the arms take about 40 to 45 min wall instead of 2.6 h.
Before the full run, delete probe/factbank.sqlite and probe/factbank_v2.sqlite (221 MB). The full run needs about 520 MB, and only 1.6 GB is free on a disk shared with other lenses.
Budget separately for the 3B model's form calls for v12 and v14: 250 new questions across the test set, the changed copy and the 3 writers. I did not time them.
risks: The times were measured while another lens was running (load average 1.4 to 2.6 on 4 CPUs), and the v1 build's 152 s was mostly cold file reads shared with two other readers. A fresh, cold set could be faster or slower.

This is a seen set (mt5k), so the scores are only a hint. The 0.859 for v13 is driven mainly by how the questions were generated ("tickets" against Linear-only answers, and reused keys), not by search alone.

Time depends on the number of aliases and on how densely documents link. mt5k has only 811 documents from linked sources (Linear, GitHub, Jira, Fireflies) out of 5,089, and 4,108 of its aliases are person names. A new 5k haystack drawn by `pool()`, which samples only linked sources, would have more aliases and denser links. Per-question time could then be higher; my guess is 1.5 to 2 times, which I did not measure.

Not checked:
- The arms v8, v9, v11, v12 and v14. v8 is assumed to cost like v4; v12 and v14 also need forms from the 3B model.
- Building the changed copy itself, which crashes. Its rename time is extrapolated from 100 documents with stand-in names.
- Code to draw a fresh 5k test set (`fresh()` caps at 50 documents) and its runtime.
- `single_writers.py` at 5k.
- Evidence quality (pieces within 2,000 or 24,000 characters).
- Each of the 8 action-item errors individually.
Fixing `named()` or the generator after these probes changes the design, so either fix has to be made and frozen before the pre-registration and before the test set is drawn.

reports.summary:
At 5,000 documents, many questions no longer have one right answer. Questions about duplicates and the word "tickets" account for most of v13's errors on the 5k haystack. In mt5k (5,089 seen documents), 9 Linear keys and 3 Jira keys each belong to 2–4 different issues, and 2 PR numbers belong to 2 PRs each, in the same repo. No key is both Linear and Jira. Meeting titles and action-item texts never repeat.

units() and questions() over all 5,089 documents give 193 questions (max_q=None, wordings from cie/docs/benchmarks/factbank_order/wordings.json, seed 48). In 5 of them the named key or PR matches more than one document. In 36 (18.7%) some key on the answer path repeats. In 25 (13%) the expected answer depends on which copy is meant. questions() silently keeps the last copy of each key (a dict overwrite). That also miscounts one person: Rohit Patel's count is expected as 3, but 4 Linear documents are assigned to him.

The bank keeps every copy as an alias. But when it resolves a link to a duplicated key, it picks one copy based on PYTHONHASHSEED. Under hash seed 0, v13 scores 0.080 on the 25 questions whose readings differ, and 19 of those 25 answers are another valid reading. Under hash seed 2 the same questions score 0.640. Across the two seeds, 14 of the 36 duplicate questions change answer, and the all-question mean moves from 0.756 to 0.828. The 157 other questions keep identical answers under both seeds.

A second ambiguity is bigger at 5k. Every person-kind wording says "tickets" without naming Linear. At mt5k, 15 of 42 person_count and 24 of 29 action-item questions ask about someone who also has Jira tickets. Their expected answer counts Linear only, while v13 counts Linear and Jira. These 39 questions score 0.433.

On the 118 questions with neither ambiguity, v13 scores 0.983 (group mean 0.987). That number is optimistic: mt5k is a seen set and the wordings are development wordings.

So the proposed rule removes most of the difficulty this probe measured at 5k. That is not because search is solved. The question kinds name their starting point by an exact identifier or a quoted title, and that lookup does not get harder with size. A linked-sources-only 5k haystack (2,960 Linear documents, drawn from seen documents) is much worse: 41% of questions touch a duplicated key and 31% have answers that differ by reading.

findings.title: Repeated keys, PR numbers, titles and action items in mt5k
findings.detail: Loaded all 5,089 mt5k documents with haystack_docs. Every repeated key belongs to different issues: titles differ in all 9 Linear cases and all 3 Jira cases, and assignees and due dates differ too. None are re-exports of one issue. The repeated values look like favourite numbers reused by whatever generated the benchmark (ENG-4821, SUP-4821, ENG-314159, #314159). PR numbers repeat within one repo ('redwood'), so 'per repo' does not separate them. Prefixes do not overlap: Linear uses ENG, PM and DES; Jira uses SUP and INT. The bank's alias table has 38 aliases carried by more than one document: 12 ticket keys, 2 '#n', 2 'pr:repo#n' and 22 'id:' deal/CRM ids, which no question names.
findings.numbers: Linear: 368 docs, 357 keys, 9 repeated (20 docs; ENG-4829 x4, ENG-4821, ENG-314159, ENG-278901, ENG-100123, ENG-246801, PM-663210, PM-15789, PM-9814 x2). Jira: 183 docs, 177 keys, 3 repeated (SUP-18421 x4, SUP-4821 x3, SUP-24871 x2). Keys in both Linear and Jira: 0. GitHub: 141 PRs, 139 numbers, 2 repeated (#874321, #82145, both repo 'redwood'). Fireflies: 119 titles, 0 repeated, 0 shared with other documents. Action items: 265 in 65 meetings, 0 repeated texts, 0 repeated (title, task) pairs.

findings.title: units()/questions() silently keep one copy (dict overwrite)
findings.detail: factbank_multi.py:214 and :282 build lin = {key: doc}, so the last document in haystack order wins. Line 215 builds tick = {**lin, **jira}, so Jira would beat Linear on a shared key (none observed). by_person (lines 217 and 284) and compare_two (line 342) read lin.values(), so a person's Linear document whose key a later document reuses disappears from their list. Concrete case: Rohit Patel holds ENG-314159 (dsid_a11cd7a8) and Mateo Alvarez holds the other ENG-314159 (dsid_a56bbe7d, kept). questions() expects person_count '3' for Rohit, but 4 Linear documents are assigned to him. The bank answers 4 and is scored wrong. issue_pr_author is protected, because its refs==1 check scans all documents.
findings.numbers: mt5k: 1 person_count expected answer wrong from the overwrite. Simulated linked-only 5k: 20 person_count and 58 action_owner_issues expected answers miscounted the same way.

findings.title: How the bank resolves a named key or PR number with several copies
findings.detail: The aliases table keeps every (alias, document) pair, so FactBank.named (engine.py:119) returns every copy. TrainedBank.entity_candidates marks each copy as named. Planner.candidates gives each copy its own start. When exactly two non-person things are named (plans.py:265), it also adds a two-start 'choice' plan, so one key with two copies looks like a choice between two things. Check rule 3 (plans.py:460) then requires plans that start from both copies and follow no link (the check is skipped if none pass). In compare_two, a key with 4 copies yields 5 named things, so no two-start compare plan exists. The 5k bank shows this: 'Which is due sooner, ENG-4829 or PM-903456?' was answered by an unrelated path plan from one copy. Links are the worse problem. bank.resolve (bank.py:223) builds alias_doc as a dict over a set of (alias, entity) pairs, so every link to a duplicated key goes to one copy chosen by set iteration order, which depends on PYTHONHASHSEED. run_order.sh does not fix the seed.
findings.numbers: Links to ENG-4821 (17 links) go to dsid_5fab80b5 (Rafael Ortiz) under hash seeds 0, 1 and 3, and to dsid_d7aeb7de (Keiko Yamamoto) under seed 2. units() keeps d7aeb7de. SUP-18421 links go to 8e77536c (seed 0), cd46e89b (seeds 1, 2) or 1980f45c (seed 3). ENG-314159 and SUP-4821 also flip between seeds. Example: 'PR #82145 links a Linear ticket. Who is its assignee?' gets Rafael Ortiz under seed 0; questions() expects Keiko Yamamoto.

findings.title: Questions over all 5,089 documents: how many touch a duplicate
findings.detail: units() gives 149 units (ticket 64, person 42, action 29, pr 14). questions(max_q=None, factbank_order wordings.json, seed 48) gives 193 questions. 'Named >1' means the key or PR the question names matches more than one document. 'On path' adds keys reached on the way: the PR's linked Linear key, the linked ticket, and every Linear document assigned to the person. 'Differs' means the expected answer changes with the copy chosen. Duplicates cluster on the link kinds because the reused keys are also the most-linked ones.
findings.numbers: Named >1: 5 (pr_issue 1, ticket_link 4). On path: 36 of 193 = 18.7% (pr_issue 9/14, ticket_link 20/64, person_count 4/42, person_first 3/35, action 0/29, compare_two 0/8, issue_pr_author 0/1). Differs: 25 (pr_issue 9, ticket_link 15, person_count 1). Simulated linked-only 5k, drawn from seen documents only (2,960 Linear, 513 Jira, 675 GitHub, 853 Fireflies): 176 repeated Linear keys (413 docs = 14%, ENG-314159 x10), 13 Jira, 10 PR numbers, 0 of 853 meeting titles repeated, 2 of 1,931 action-item texts repeated; 1,676 questions, named >1 172 (10%), on path 693 (41%), differs 520 (31%).

findings.title: v13 at 5k: the duplicate questions are coin flips decided by the hash seed
findings.detail: Built the mt5k bank with text facts (16 s, 115 MB) and asked all 193 questions with mdtrain/plan_lessons_v13.json, fb50/lessons.json and the glossary (no form, no Ollama). Then rebuilt the bank under PYTHONHASHSEED=2 and asked again. Questions with no duplicate on their path got identical answers under both seeds.
findings.numbers: Seed 0: duplicate questions whose readings differ (25) score 0.080, and 19 of 25 answers equal another reading's answer; duplicate questions whose readings agree (11) score 1.000; questions with no duplicate (157) score 0.846. Seed 2: the same 25 score 0.640; the 157 still score 0.846. Answers changed between seeds: 14 of 36 duplicate questions, 0 of 157 others. All-question mean 0.756 (seed 0) vs 0.828 (seed 2). Time per question: median 2.5 s, max 7.1 s; 515–520 s for 193 questions.

findings.title: A second ambiguity at scale: 'tickets' means Linear only, or Linear and Jira
findings.detail: All 6 person-kind wordings in wordings.json say 'tickets' and name no tracker. Expected answers count Linear issues only; the v11/v13 ticket rule counts Linear and Jira. At 5k, many of the people asked about also hold Jira tickets. Every clean person_count failure (15) is exactly the Linear+Jira count, for example Priya Nair answered 6 against an expected 3 (3 Linear + 3 Jira). The action-item failures list INT- and SUP- keys alongside the expected Linear keys. person_first is unaffected because the Jira records have no due_date.
findings.numbers: mt5k: 15 of 42 person_count and 24 of 29 action questions have two readings, none caught by the duplicate rule (39 questions; v13 0.433 on them). Simulated linked-only 5k: 64 more such questions beyond the duplicate rule.

findings.title: Without either ambiguity, v13 is almost perfect at 5k on this seen set
findings.detail: Removing the duplicate questions and the tracker-reading questions leaves 118 questions, which v13 answers almost perfectly. The 59 person questions whose wording also matches a first-name-only person did no harm (person_first 1.000). Caveat: mt5k contains mdtrain (v13's training set), mdtest, fb50 and fbtest, and the wordings are the order test's development wordings, so these numbers are optimistic.
findings.numbers: Group mean (link/combine/compare): all 193 questions 0.826 (plain mean 0.756); dropping duplicate questions 0.912 (n=157, link 0.96); dropping both ambiguities 0.987 (n=118, plain mean 0.983, combine 1.0, link 0.96, compare 1.0).

findings.title: A 50-document question set placed in the 5k haystack changes expected answers
findings.detail: mdtrain and mdtest lie inside mt5k. Regenerated their questions inside the 50 documents (default wordings, seeds 11 and 12; their questions.jsonl was not read) and recomputed every expected answer over all 5,089 documents. All 8 of mdtest's pr_issue questions go through ENG-4821. Expected answers must be computed over the whole haystack, never inside a 50-document unit set.
findings.numbers: mdtrain: 3 of 48 change (2 from duplicates; 1 because a second PR referencing the key exists at 5k). mdtest: 13 of 50 change (11 from duplicates; 2 from more documents, e.g. a ticket that now links 2 tickets, and a person count going from 3 to 4).

findings.title: Person names: one name, several people
findings.detail: Questions name people by full name. One name clearly covers several different people: Jordan Lee appears at acme.com, bridgepoint.ai, omniretail.com, zendiq.com and gmail.com; Maya Chen carries 9 role labels. The bank merges people by lowercased name, so namesakes' relations attach to one person entity. Linear assignee fields hold bare names, so it cannot be told whether two internal people share a name. A separate problem appears only at scale: action-item owners create first-name-only people ('Ethan', 'Priya', and even 'ENG-86001'). named() then matches them inside full names ('person:ethan' inside 'Ethan Morales').
findings.numbers: 4,048 distinct names in people fields; 246 with more than one email; 88 with more than one role label. Of the 42 people asked about: 12 also appear with a non-Redwood email domain, 20 share their name with external or customer contacts, 15 are also Jira assignees. 116 of 394 internal tracker names are also used for external contacts. First-name-only people: 62 in the 5k bank (all action-item owners); 927 full names contain one; named() returns two people for 32/42 person_count and 27/35 person_first questions. Earlier 50-document banks have 0–6 such people and 0–5 affected names.

findings.title: The duplicate rule removes the most-linked items
findings.detail: The reused keys are also the keys most documents link to (partly because several issues share one key string). Dropping questions on duplicated keys therefore removes the hub targets, and the kept set is easier on fan-in.
findings.numbers: Median documents linking to the target key, dropped vs kept. mt5k: pr_issue 26 vs 4; ticket_link 8 vs 1.5 (kept max 12). Simulated linked-only 5k: pr_issue 64 vs 6; ticket_link 13 vs 3 (kept max 47).

findings.title: A rule based on gold documents is not enough
findings.detail: Rule A drops a question if any of its gold documents carries a repeated key or PR number. It misses the people who lost a document to the overwrite, because the lost document is not among their gold documents. The rule must check every Linear document in the haystack assigned to the person.
findings.numbers: mt5k: rule A drops 34, rule B (whole answer path) drops 36; the 2 missed are person_count-036 (whose expected answer is wrong) and person_first-037. Simulated linked-only 5k: rule A drops 628, rule B 693 (A misses 37 action, 15 person_count, 13 person_first).

recommendations: Pre-register a 'one meaning per name' rule, applied by code after the questions are drawn and before any arm runs. H = every document the 5k bank is built from. Over H count: K(k) = Linear+Jira documents whose raw 'key' (upper case) is k; P(n) = GitHub documents whose 'pr_number' is n, in any repo; M(t) = Fireflies documents whose title normalises to t; A(t) = parsed action items whose text normalises to t. Compute expected answers over H, mapping each key to all its documents (no dict overwrite). Drop a question if: U1 (named) a key it names has K != 1, a PR number it names has P != 1, its quoted meeting title has M != 1, or its quoted action item has A != 1; U2 (reached) a key the answer goes through has K != 1 (pr_issue: the PR's linked Linear key; ticket_link: the linked ticket's key; person_count, person_first, action_owner_issues: the key of every Linear document in H assigned to that person, not just the gold documents); U3 (tracker) a person_count, person_first or action_owner_issues question that names no tracker (NAMES_TRACKER) and whose Linear-only answer differs from its Linear+Jira answer.

Report: questions drawn, dropped by U1, then U2, then U3, and kept per kind. Declare a per-kind floor below which a kind is 'not measurable'. Draw with max_q=None, filter, then cap to the target count in a pre-declared order, so drops do not empty a kind. Expected drops: about 19% by U1+U2 and another about 20% by U3 in a source mix like mt5k; about 41% by U1+U2 in a linked-sources-only 5k.

Fix PYTHONHASHSEED (for example 0) for every bank build and record it. Add one check to the pre-registration: kept-question answers must be identical under PYTHONHASHSEED=0 and 1 for one arm (this probe found 0 of 157 changed).

As secondary measures, score all drawn questions two ways: strict (as questions() drew them) and lenient (right if the answer matches any reading). This bounds how much the rule moves the result and keeps the hub questions visible.

State plainly in the pre-registration that U1–U3 remove questions with no single right answer, not search difficulty. In this probe they also removed almost all of v13's 5k errors (0.983 on the 118 that remain), because every kind names its start by an exact key, PR number or quoted title. If the 5k test is meant to show 'where search is hard', it needs questions whose start must be found by content. This rule leaves that difficulty, and the first-name and namesake problems, untouched.

Do not drop questions for first-name-only alias matches or for namesakes (one name used by several people). The question is well-defined there; matching the right person is the bank's job. Report them as diagnostics: how many questions where named() returns more than one person.

If a 50-document question set is embedded among 5k distractors, recompute every expected answer over the full haystack and apply U1–U3 over the full haystack. Expected answers computed inside the 50 documents changed for 3 of 48 (mdtrain) and 13 of 50 (mdtest) questions.
Run the duplicate counts on the actual test haystack once it is chosen. The rates depend heavily on how many tracker documents it holds.
risks: mt5k is a seen set: mdtrain, mdtest, fb50 and fbtest lie inside it, v13 was trained on mdtrain's questions, and wordings.json holds the order test's development wordings. The 0.983 and 0.846 scores are optimistic and are not a test result.
Selection bias: U2 removes the most-linked targets (pr_issue median 26 vs 4 incoming links), so the kept set is easier on fan-in. pr_issue may fall below any sensible floor (5 of 14 kept at mt5k).

U3 replaces the open question of what 'tickets' means with a drop. Dropping is neutral between v9 (Linear only) and v11+ (Linear+Jira). Defining 'tickets' as Linear+Jira instead would change the question definition from earlier tests and favour v11+.

The drop rates depend strongly on the haystack's mix: 19% (mixed, 368 Linear documents) vs 41% (linked-only, 2,960 Linear documents). A haystack built only from linked sources could lose most questions.

Without a fixed PYTHONHASHSEED, any bank rebuild changes scores on duplicate questions (all-question mean 0.756 vs 0.828 here). The earlier 50-document runs were exposed to the same issue, but duplicates within 50 documents were rare.

The per-question times (median 2.5 s, max 7.1 s, about 8.5 min for 193 questions with v13) came from a shared 4-CPU machine with other probes running. Arms using the 3B form via Ollama (v12, v14) were not timed.

reports.summary:
Recommendation: build the 5,000-document test by nesting. Draw a new 50-document set exactly as in earlier tests (build_fresh with a new seed, all 15 earlier folders excluded). Then add 4,950 distractors from every source, each source in its share of the remaining documents, and skip the few distractors that would change an answer. The same 50 questions are then asked on the 50-document set and on the 5,000-document set, so the effect of size is a per-question paired difference. This needs one new function and changes no default behaviour.

Simulated on lexsample, a sample of 200,001 documents that are seen and already excluded. With the skip rules, 49-50 of 49-50 questions kept their expected answer in 10 draws; without them, only 29-40 of 50 did, across 4 draws.

What rules out the other options:
- A plain stratified 5,000-document sample starves the pull-request kinds: pr_issue 1-4 and issue_pr_author 1-2 in all 5 draws.
- Planting 8 units of each kind fresh()-style, then adding filler, still gives issue_pr_author only 1-5. The filler breaks planted units. The 50 questions come mostly from units that arose by chance, so planting the non-PR kinds adds nothing.
- A secondary option works: a stratified sample with ticket keys unique, plus 10 protected PR-to-issue pairs, with questions over the whole set. It gave exactly 8/7/7/7/7/7/7 per kind in 8 of 8 draws with the default questions().

The changed copy does not scale: at 5,000 documents factbank_split.changed crashes. There are 4,200 people to rename and only 560 new names.

The union of haystack.json dsids of mt5k, mt50, fb50, fbtest, mdtrain, mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdplan, mdrep, mdtick, mdord and lexsample is 205,487. findings.title: Option A, a plain stratified 5,000 over all sources: the pull-request kinds starve
findings.detail:
Five draws from lexsample (seeds 101-105), with questions over the whole set and default questions(). Ticket, person and action units arise naturally in large numbers; PR units barely do. Why:
- Most PRs link 2 keys, and a PR counts as a unit only if exactly one of them is in the set.
- Most PRs link no key that exists as a Linear document in lexsample.
- Popular keys are referenced by many PRs, so the author question, which needs exactly one referencing PR, fails.
- Ticket links concentrate on hubs: up to 11 units point to the same 'to' ticket, almost all through linear.dependencies.
findings.numbers: Units per draw: person 26-38, ticket 34-42, action 16-27, pr 1-4. Default 50 questions: pr_issue 1-4, issue_pr_author 1-2, action 10, person_count 9-10, person_first 9-10, ticket_link 9-10, compare_two 8. In lexsample's 3,116 PRs: 2,777 link 2 keys; 2,082 link no existing Linear key; ENG-4821 is referenced by 162 PRs.

findings.title: Option B, units first (fresh()-style, 8 per kind) then unprotected filler: does not fix it
findings.detail:
Five draws (seeds 201-205). Units were planted from a pool() sample of about 2,318 linked documents, then filled to the source targets. Two problems:
- The filler breaks planted units: people gain issues, PRs gain a second in-set key or a second referencing PR.
- The default cap takes units in dsid order among all units, so most of the 50 questions come from units that arose by chance.
findings.numbers: issue_pr_author 1-5, pr_issue 7-8. Planted units surviving (fraction of planted that remained units): person 8/16-11/15, action 4/9-8/9, pr 4/8-8/8, ticket 9/10-14/14. Questions from planted units: pr_issue 3-5, other kinds 0-3.

findings.title: Option B3: stratified sample, unique ticket keys, plus 10 protected PR-to-issue pairs
findings.detail:
Eligible pair: a PR with a number of 3+ digits and an author who is a person, linking key k, where k is on exactly one candidate Linear document and exactly one candidate PR links it.
The filler skips:
- Linear or Jira documents whose key is already in the set;
- Linear documents whose key is another link of a planted PR.
Questions over the whole 5,000 with the default questions().
findings.numbers: 8 of 8 draws (seeds 401-408) gave exactly action 8 and 7 each for the other six kinds. PR units 10-14; issue_pr_author candidates 10-12. Filler skipped 3-9 documents per draw. 0 duplicate keys in any set. Eligible pairs in lexsample: 94 of 3,116 PRs; not counted on the remaining documents.

findings.title: Option C (recommended): the usual 50-document set nested in 5,000, its questions unchanged
findings.numbers: Without the skips: 29, 31, 29 and 40 of 49-50 questions stay valid; person_count keeps 2-4 of 5-7, action 3-8 of 8-9, issue_pr_author 3-4 of 4-6, compare_two 5-7 of 8. With the skips: 49/49 or 50/50 in 4 draws, and again in 6 draws. Documents skipped per draw: 14-26 (duplicate key 6-11, a question person's issues 2-12, PR linking a question's issue 2-8, other links 0-2). Jira tickets of question people left in the 5,000: 0-3 per draw. Question PR numbers shared with another PR: 0.

findings.title: Duplicate ticket keys are a hazard at 5,000 that units() and questions() do not handle
findings.detail:
Many Linear documents share a key with a different issue (different title, assignee or due date). units() and questions() build lin = {key: doc}, so the doc later in dsid order silently replaces the earlier one:
- expected answers can come from either document;
- person counts drop the overwritten issue.
At 50 documents this is rare. At 5,000 it occurs in every draw, and a filler that keeps keys unique removes it. PR numbers and meeting titles are not a problem at this size.
findings.numbers: lexsample: 1,648 Linear keys on 2+ documents; 4,836 of 13,763 Linear documents share a key; one key is on 40 documents. Jira: 151 such keys. 5,000-document draws: 1-6 Linear documents overwritten per set. PR numbers: 205 numbers on 2+ PRs in lexsample, 0-1 per 5,000-document set. Meeting titles: 3,962 distinct of 3,962.

findings.title: The 2-4 person window still yields plenty of person units at 5,000, but skips the busiest people
findings.detail: Person units survive at 5,000: 26-47 per draw. But the window excludes people with 5 or more issues in the set, who hold 42% of all Linear issues there, and their action items. Answers are closed-world: the people asked about have 2-4 issues in the slice but dozens across the company. In B3 draws, person_count answers are mostly 2.
findings.numbers: Per draw (mean over 8 B3 draws): 114 people with 1 issue, 33.5 with 2-4, 10 with 5-8, 5.6 with 9+. Maximum per person in plain draws: 20-33. Issues held by people with 5+: 1,152 of 2,752. Action items by the owner's in-set issue count: 0 71%, 1 13%, 2-4 12%, 5+ 5%. Company-wide (lexsample): 1,566 assignees, median 1 issue, p90 11, max 946. The 31 people asked about in one 5,000-document draw have a median of 72 issues in lexsample; 87% have 10 or more. person_count answers over all units: 2 = 60%, 3 = 25%, 4 = 15%.

findings.title: How questions()'s cap behaves and what it biases
findings.detail:
The default output is exactly the interleave of questions(..., max_q=None); this held on all 8 draws. So a new selector can post-process the uncapped list without touching questions().
- With every kind at 8 or more, the cap gives action_owner_issues 8 (first alphabetically) and 7 for each other kind, compare_two included (7 of its 8). Groups: link 21, combine 22, compare 7.
- Within a kind, units come in dsid order. A person unit's position is the smallest dsid among their issues, so people with 4 issues come early more often than people with 2.
- Action units of the same meeting sit next to each other, so the same owners repeat.
- compare_two pairs come from a seeded shuffle of all dated issues; no bias found there.
findings.numbers: Over 8 B3 draws: people with 4 issues are 29% of capped person_count questions (16 of 56) against 15% of all units (41 of 268). Distinct action answers: 39 of 64 capped, 63 of 64 with a seeded shuffle within each kind plus new targets first. issue_pr_author distinct answers 53 → 56; ticket_link 34 → 38.

findings.title: An optional author-aware PR choice in fresh() balances the kinds (option C)
findings.detail: Variant: PR units with distinct issues, the issue referenced by only that PR in the pool, and an author who is a person. This would be a new optional flag; fresh()'s default stays as it is. Compared over 10 seeds (601-610) on lexsample pools.
findings.numbers: issue_pr_author mean 3.8 (min 1) → 6.8 (min 5); pr_issue 7.8 → 6.7; ticket_link 6.9 → 5.7; total questions 491 → 498 of 500. With plain fresh(), 3 of 10 seeds fell short of 50 questions (46-48).

findings.title: The changed copy does not scale as it is
findings.detail:
factbank_split.changed on a 5,000-document probe (a lexsample draw, deleted afterwards) stops with IndexError at factbank_split.py line 193. Its new-name pool is FIRST × LAST = 28 × 20 = 560 names, and a 5,000-document set has 4,200 people. Parts were timed separately because a run with a monkeypatched 27,600-name pool spent minutes on the corpus check alone.
- Ordering names longest first prevents one name replacing part of a longer one. It does not respect word boundaries.
- The 50-document and 5,000-document copies would give the same person different new names unless one mapping is shared.
findings.numbers: People to rename: 4,200; new names available: 560. Corpus check: 13 ms per candidate name on a 28 MB corpus (560 names in 7.3 s). Renaming: 0.10 s per document, about 8.5 minutes per 5,000-document copy on one core. 353 of 4,200 names sit inside another person's name. Output: 28.6 MB per copy. Loading 5,000 documents with haystack_docs takes 2.1 s; units() 0.04 s; questions() 0.03 s.

recommendations: Primary procedure, the paired nested design (option C). (1) Exclude all 15 folders listed (205,487 documents). (2) Make the 50-document core with the existing build_fresh(index, root, exclude_dirs, out=<core>, seed=<new seed, not 13/17/29/31/37/41/42/43/47>, wordings=<pre-registered>). (3) Widen it with a new function, e.g. widen(core_dir, index_path, root, exclude_dirs, out, n=5000, seed). Per-source targets come from the remaining shares (slack 2,796; gmail 1,188; linear 341; google_drive 245; hubspot 147; fireflies 98; github 77; jira 59; confluence 49), minus the core's documents of that source. Shuffle each source with the seed and skip any document that would change an answer: a Linear or Jira key already in the set; another link of a question's PR or from-ticket; a Linear or Jira item assigned to a question's person or action owner; a GitHub PR linking a question's Linear key or sharing a question's PR number. (4) Copy questions.jsonl byte for byte, recheck every question's expected answer at 5,000 and stop if any changed. Write haystack.json with the core dsids and the skip counts.

Run every arm on both the 50-document core and the 5,000-document set with the same questions. The pre-registered measure is the per-question paired difference (5,000 minus 50) per arm, alongside the earlier rules. The core run also counts as one more 50-document replication.

For the kind mix, keep fresh() and questions() defaults. If about 7-8 author questions are wanted, add an optional flag to fresh() or a new fresh2() that chooses PR units with distinct issues referenced by only that PR in the pool (simulated: issue_pr_author mean 3.8 → 6.8, min 1 → 5). Decide before drawing.

If questions over the whole 5,000 are wanted instead, or as a second set, use option B3: a stratified sample of all sources with Linear and Jira keys unique, plus 10 planted PR-to-issue pairs, each issue on one candidate Linear document and referenced by one candidate PR, protected from the filler. Generate questions with questions(..., max_q=None) and pick 50 with a new selector, e.g. pick(qs, n=50, seed, distinct=True): seeded shuffle within each kind, new targets first, then the same interleave. This removes the dsid-order bias toward people with 4 issues (29% vs 15%) and repeated action owners (39 vs 63 distinct of 64). The default cap still gives 8/7/7/7/7/7/7 if you prefer it.
Make every 5,000-document set key-unique for Linear and Jira. Otherwise 1-6 documents per set are silently overwritten by units() and questions(), and some expected answers are arbitrary.

Fix the changed copy without changing its default: add an optional name pool of at least about 6,000 synthetic names, checked against the corpus (about 80 s at 13 ms per name), or an option to pass a name mapping. Share one mapping between the core's and the 5,000's changed copies so the two stay paired. Expect about 8.5 minutes of renaming per 5,000-document copy unless renaming moves to a single compiled regex, and about 29 MB on disk per copy.

In the pre-registration, report: the always-answer-2 baseline on person_count (about 52-60% of person_count questions in the B3 draws); jira_people (0-3 Jira tickets of question people at 5,000 unless protected); the number of skipped distractors; and that answers are computed within the set (people asked about have a median of 72 issues company-wide but 2-4 in the set).

Before drawing, count the eligible PR pairs (B3) or confirm fresh()'s yield (C) on the remaining documents, and stop with an error if there are fewer than 10. This lens did not read the remaining documents.
risks: Feasibility numbers (unit counts, eligible PR pairs, how many questions survive, skip counts) come from lexsample, a seen 39% sample, as a stand-in. The remaining 306,471 documents were counted by source only. Earlier md* sets took about 500 linked documents out of the pool; those were left out of the estimates, though it should matter little.

The protections in C and B3 bias the distractors slightly: 14-26 documents tied to the questions' entities are skipped (3-9 in B3). The people asked about therefore have no extra issues in the 5,000, although company-wide they have dozens. A method cannot see this, but it should be stated.

The 2-4 window (kept for comparability) never asks about the busiest people, who hold 42% of Linear issues at 5,000 documents. A count or list over 5 or more items is untested. Widening it would be a new optional parameter and a different test.

Option C's questions all come from a 50-document cluster, so some question kinds stay underfilled as in earlier tests (issue_pr_author can be 1-2 without the author-aware variant; ticket_link 2-11). With about 7 questions per kind, the per-kind numbers are noisy.

The changed copy at 5,000 cannot run with the current code (IndexError). Renaming 4,200 names by substring risks partial replacements: 353 names sit inside another name, and word boundaries are not checked.

Not checked: building banks or running any arm at 5,000 (time and memory belong to the scale lens); name ambiguity, such as two people with the same name, or keys mentioned in Slack or Gmail (the ambiguity lens); wordings; the original single-document fact-bank test that FACTBANK_RESULTS.md also lists as owed (mt5k holds 243 such questions, but mt5k is seen); and whether dsid order is unrelated to content beyond the measured person-count bias.

Probe scripts and small result files are kept under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/u5k/draw/: sim_random.py, sim_plant.py, sim_b2.py, sim_b3.py, sim_nested.py, nested_extra.py, fresh2.py, bias.py, dupkeys.py, prpairs.py, changed_cost.py and *.json, 136 KB in all. All probe data (the pickles, the 5,000-document probe folder and its changed copy) were deleted. No repository file was modified, and nothing in the remaining 306,471 documents beyond index paths was read.

reports.summary:
Protocol lens. I propose a 5,000-document test in which only the bank size changes. It has a decisive comparison inside the test: the same 50 questions and expected answers, asked of a bank of only their gold documents (about 80 docs) and of the full ~5,000-doc bank.

1. **The control is valid.** On mt5k probes, all 50 expected answers computed in the 5k set came out the same from the gold-doc union, for two seeds' draws (48 and 1).
2. **Two filters are needed.** At 5k some expected answers become ill-defined:
   - J: the order test's wordings say "tickets", but expected answers count Linear issues only, and at 5k many people also have Jira tickets.
   - K: ticket keys and PR numbers are reused across documents (ENG-4821 sits on 2 Linear docs and is linked by 9 PRs).

   On a seen mt5k probe, v13 fell from 1.000 (82-doc bank) to 0.859 (5,089-doc bank). Every one of its 15 losses is a flagged question: 12 J, 3 K. On the 21 unflagged questions v13 scored 1.000 at both sizes. Under a "Linear plus Jira" reading, its 5k answers on all 16 J questions are fully right.
3. **The cost is real.** v13 takes a median of 4.3 s per question at 5k against 0.2 s at 82 docs. The 5k bank file is 115 MB.
4. **The original FACTBANK test should be a separate part B.** Its fact-bank evidence collapses at 5k: the answer is within the first 2,000 characters for 0.226 of questions against 0.767 at 50 docs, and within 24,000 characters for 0.745 against 0.987. But the present memory bank needs Postgres, which is down (not running, as the brief said), plus a 5,089-doc load with vectors and roughly 400 MB of disk on a disk with 1.6–1.8 GB free.

All probes ran on seen sets (mt5k, lexsample). They tell us about the design and the thresholds, not the test result.

findings.title: The in-test control (b) is valid: expected answers computed at 5k come out the same from the gold-doc union
findings.detail:
**From the code (`questions()`):**
- `inside` is the whole 5k set.
- A person question's `gold_docs` is every Linear doc in `by_person[p]` over the 5k, so a count or first-due question already holds all of that person's issues.
- An action item's gold is the meeting plus all the owner's issues.
- A link question's gold is the two linked docs.
- A compare question's gold is the two issues.
- The small set is a subset of the 5k, so a person's issues in the small set are exactly that list.

**Empirically on mt5k (5,089 docs):**
- Seed 48: 50 of 50 the same once matched by kind, field, gold docs and identifiers. My first check showed one false difference (`ticket_link-status-078`): the reverse ticket unit has the same gold docs, so my lookup key collided.
- Seed 1: 50 of 50 the same.
- A per-question check against each question's own gold docs alone gave 190 of 193 the same. The 3 differences were the same lookup artefact, not re-checked with the identifier key.

**Small-bank size:** 81 docs (seed 48) and 82 (seed 1); 78–83 in fresh-like probe draws. That is close to the 50-doc tests, whose banks were also only the units' documents.

**What it means:** the 50-doc test is reproduced inside the 5k test, on identical questions and expected answers.
findings.numbers: 50/50 (seed 48), 50/50 (seed 1); small bank 81–82 docs on mt5k, 78–83 in probes; 82-doc bank: 563 entities, 3,858 facts, 3.26 MB, built in 1.15 s

findings.title: At 5k some expected answers are ill-defined: Jira owners (J) and reused keys or PR numbers (K)
findings.detail:
**J (Jira owners).**
- The order test's writers name no tracker, so their wordings say "tickets". v11 and later read that as Linear or Jira.
- `questions()` counts Linear issues only.
- In a 50-doc bank this rarely matters. At 5k many people asked about also have Jira tickets assigned.

**K (reused identifiers).**
- The benchmark reuses ticket keys, so one key or PR number can sit on several documents.
- The generator keeps the last document in dict order, so the expected answer is arbitrary.
- mt5k has 12 of 534 keys and 2 of 139 PR numbers shared by more than one doc.
- ENG-4821 sits on 2 Linear docs and is linked by 9 PRs; 9 of mt5k's 14 PR units go through it.

**Counts on mt5k (seed-1 questions):** 16 J, 13 K, 21 clean. mt5k is enriched with gold and linked docs (183 Jira docs).

**Fresh-like draws** (lexsample, core plus distractors, about 58–60 Jira docs):
- the drawn 50 had K 2–4 and J 0–6;
- 137–156 clean questions were available;
- a clean 50 keeps all 7 kinds, with `issue_pr_author` 2–6.

**Filters, from raw fields only** (`u5k/protocol/filters.py`):
- K: every key and PR number in the question, its pieces and its expected IDs is carried by exactly one doc in the 5k.
- J: for count, first-due and action-item questions, the person has no Jira doc with them as assignee in the 5k.
findings.numbers: mt5k (seed 1): K 13, J 16, clean 21 of 50. mt5k (seed 48): 12 of 50 ambiguous by K. Probe seeds 901/902/903: drawn-50 K 4/4/2, J 1/0/6; clean pools 147/156/137

findings.title: Probe on mt5k (seen): every v13 loss at 5k is on a flagged question
findings.detail:
Same 50 questions (seed 1, order-test wordings), asked of the 82-doc gold bank and the 5,089-doc bank.

**All 50 questions:** see the scores below.

**The 21 clean questions:** see the scores below. Right for the right reason on the clean set: v13 1.000 at both sizes; v9 and v11 0.944 at both sizes.

**v13's 15 losses:**
- 8 action items, which gained the owner's Jira keys;
- 4 count questions, which counted Jira tickets too;
- 3 reused-key questions.

Under the Linear plus Jira reading, v13's 5k answers on all 16 J questions score 1.0.

Of the 3 reused-key losses, 2 are wrong under either document: `pr_issue-085` answered with an account field, and `ticket_link-092` answered its own key. The third, `ticket_link-086`, gave the other document's assignee. So key reuse is a real hazard for the bank at scale, not only a scoring artefact.

**First names:** the 5k bank also finds first-name-only people (person:jordan, person:priya, ...) in 14 of 16 count and first-due questions. On clean questions the planner still chose the full name.

**Order of arms at 5k (all 50):** v13 > v11 > v9 > v4 > v8. v8 is below v4 at both sizes here, while on the order test v8 0.742 > v4 0.647. So v8 vs v4 should not be a rule.

findings.title: How to draw the haystack: a pure random 5k has no PR-linked questions; core plus distractors gives all 7 kinds
findings.detail:
Probes inside lexsample (seen, excluded from tests), probe seeds only.

**(A) Stratified 5,000 from all sources:** 0 PR units, so no `pr_issue` or `issue_pr_author` questions. The link group would be `ticket_link` alone. Not comparable with the 50-doc tests.

**(B) The earlier tests' core plus distractors:**
- core = `fresh(pool(...))`, 50 docs of whole units;
- plus 4,950 distractors stratified over all 9 sources;
- result: all 7 kinds and 171–185 questions.
- Only 12–16 of a clean 50 come wholly from the core. The rest come from units formed inside the haystack, all valid because the answers are computed over the 5k.

**Kind mix:**
- At 5k, `issue_pr_author` is scarce (needs exactly one referencing PR): 1 of 14 PR units in mt5k, 2–6 in probes.
- So the kind mix differs from the 50-doc tests (order test: `issue_pr_author` 8).
- Comparison (a) must therefore be by kind.

**Pool:**
- Excluded: 205,487 docs (the 15 folders, now including mdord).
- Remaining: 306,471 docs, by source as below.

findings.title: Cost at 5k: build, storage, time per question
findings.detail:

critic.summary:
Completeness critic. The four reports mostly design a 5,000-document version of the multi-document planner test. That is not the check the docs say is owed. FACTBANK_RESULTS.md (lines 45 and 92) owes "the same test on the 5,000-document haystack, where search is hard": the original comparison of the fact bank against the memory bank, scored on whether the answer appears within 2,000, 6,000 or 24,000 characters of evidence, on owner, deadline and list questions. Only the protocol lens covers it, as "part B", and it defers that part. Task #98 is titled "fact bank and planner", so the design has to cover both parts, or the user has to choose.

I checked three claims myself.
1. **The protocol lens's key filter misses a known case.** On mt5k's 193 questions (seed 48), the filters keep person_count-036 (Rohit Patel). Its expected answer is 3, but he has 4 Linear documents, because questions() keeps only the last document for each key (factbank_multi.py:282). The ambiguity lens's U2 rule does catch it.
2. **Bank builds are not reproducible run to run.** bank.resolve (bank.py:223) builds a dict from a set, so which copy of a reused key wins depends on Python's hash seed. No script or doc sets PYTHONHASHSEED. The probe scores on reused-key questions came from builds with an unrecorded seed.
3. **Exclusions are clean.** The excluded union is 205,487 documents. All five haystacks under u5k, and all 29 derived top-level folders, lie inside it, so no remaining document has leaked.

The lenses also disagree on several design points that must be settled before anything is frozen:
- how to handle ambiguous questions: skip distractor documents (drawing), drop questions with filters K and J (protocol), or drop with rules U1 to U3 (ambiguity);
- which bank is the control: the 50-document core, or the union of the questions' gold documents;
- whether the changed copy and the three single-writer sets are in scope;
- whether any code changes before the freeze (named(), factbank_split, the generator).

The biggest risk is that the planner part passes by construction. Every question kind names its start by an exact key, PR number, quoted title or full name. Every proposed rule removes the hub keys and the people who also hold Jira tickets. On the questions left, v13 scored 1.000 (protocol lens, 21 questions) and 0.983 (ambiguity lens, 118 questions) on seen sets. A pass would show that unrelated documents do not hurt. It would not show that search holds up when it is hard. Part B is where a real effect appears: the fact bank's 2,000-character reach fell from 0.767 to 0.226 at 5k, which is below the memory bank's 0.375 at 50 documents. But part B needs Postgres (down) and a 5,089-document tenant, and its fact-bank side has already been looked at.

findings.title: VERIFIED: bank builds depend on Python's hash seed, and nothing fixes it
findings.detail:
How it happens:
- bank.py:87 declares `aliases: set[tuple[str, str]]`.
- resolve() at bank.py:223 builds `alias_doc = {a: e for a, e in b.aliases ...}`.
- When a key belongs to several documents, the copy that wins depends on set iteration order. String hashing is randomized per process, so the order changes from run to run.

What I checked:
- `grep PYTHONHASHSEED docs src` finds nothing.
- run_order.sh does not set it.

Consequences:
- The scale and protocol probes, which share one pair of mt5k banks, were built with an unrecorded seed. Their '3 reused-key losses' could be different under another seed.
- The ambiguity lens measured the all-question mean at 0.756 under seed 0 and 0.828 under seed 2.
- The other lenses do not mention this at all.
- Other places where order depends on the hash seed (for example ties broken by set order in the planner) were not audited.

findings.title: Three incompatible ways to handle ambiguity, and each one makes the test easier
findings.detail:
(1) Drawing lens, option C: skip distractor documents that would change an answer.
- These include the question people's Linear and Jira items, PRs that link question keys, and duplicate keys.
- The neighbourhood of each question entity in the 5k haystack is therefore artificially clean.

(2) Protocol lens: drop questions with K or J.
- J drops every person, count or action question whose person has any Jira ticket, even person_first, where Jira has no due_date and the answer cannot differ.

(3) Ambiguity lens: drop with U1, U2 and U3.
- U3 drops only when the Linear-only answer differs from the Linear plus Jira answer.

What they share:
- All three remove the hub targets (median incoming links 26 dropped against 4 kept for pr_issue).
- All three remove the people whose Jira tickets create the 'tickets' ambiguity.
- The kept set is biased toward easy questions.

The alternatives are not neutral either:
- Defining 'tickets' as Linear plus Jira favours v11 and later.
- Keeping the questions and scoring them leniently (any valid reading) treats both readings as right.

The design must pick one rule, apply it in code, and report what it drops.

- named() returns every copy of an alias, and the bank's alias table holds every pair.

What the probes show after the filters:
- v13 scored 1.000 at both sizes on the 21 clean questions (protocol lens).
- v13 scored 0.983 on 118 clean questions (ambiguity lens).
- v9 and v11 scored 0.972 at both sizes.

So the decisive rules R1 (5k minus small ≥ −0.05) and R2 (≥ 0.95) are likely to be met. A pass would mean 'unrelated documents do not break exact lookups'. It would not mean 'search holds at scale'.

The real 5k hazards left in the clean questions:
- first-name-only people: 62 in the bank, and named() returns two people for 32 of 42 person_count questions;
- namesakes;
- candidate plans growing from about 30 to about 586 per question.

Part B (the original fact bank against memory bank test, rules 1 to 4, on owner, deadline and list questions) is the check FACTBANK_RESULTS.md owes, and it is the one where search gets hard. Part A (the planner at 5k) mainly tests robustness to distractors. If part B cannot run locally (Postgres down, 5,089-document tenant, about 400 MB, embedding), plan it on Colab with notebooks/memory_test_colab.ipynb rather than dropping it.
